doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: Cutting at an angle and protecting a nervous second engineer
summary: Hank explains angled splices and how he quietly made the cut himself rather than pressure a new second engineer.

blocks.x: Did you cut at an angle?
And what is the reason for that?
So that it runs smoothly across the heads.

You know what I mean? First of all you shouldn’t ever have a problem if you make a cut and put it together and if you’re a good engineer and a good editor you’re going to make it once and it’s not going to be — if you’re not good and you missed the downbeat and some second guy doesn’t know what he’s doing and he lost the tape because he put the — you know if you’re the engineer that’s running the date you’ve got to make sure that while everybody’s talking, with one ear on what the second guy’s doing to make that cut. And if you’re not sure of him being able to make the cut I have done many times, © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

because I know that the second engineer is a new guy, he’s a little nervous about making a cut on a date, I would never say a word. I’d just go and make the cut myself. I don’t want to put that guy under any kind of pressure. And luckily I worked with a lot of great engineers when I was coming up and that’s the way they operated, that’s the way they worked. Until they got comfortable with you, or I got comfortable with the second to make him make the edit, you know. But if I wasn’t sure about the guy making the edit I don’t want him to take the wrong take you know. Like you say put — I’m keeping the first chorus from the this take and the second chorus from take 12. You’d better make sure that he knows where he’s going and the whole control room is talking at the same time. You know? And you’ve got to keep them talking and pay attention, but the other ear is listening to where the second guy is going.
